passage: Anjali, you look worried about your exams, so let me tell you what I did at sixteen. I'm Ramesh. Everyone told me how to score well: study more, study harder. That wasn't helping, so I turned it around and asked, 'What would guarantee I do badly?' I wrote the list on the back of my timetable: cramming all night before the paper, skipping sleep, never looking at past papers, sitting with my phone beside my book, leaving my weakest chapter for last. Then I built my routine to dodge each one. Lights out by eleven. Two past papers every Sunday. Phone in the other room. Weakest chapter first, on Monday. My mother read the list on my wall and quietly stopped calling me for late tea. It looked boring on paper, but in the exam hall I felt awake and knew the shape of the paper.

qa.q: At what time was lights out in Ramesh's routine?
What was Ramesh feeling about the advice to study more and study harder?
qa.a: Ramesh felt unhelped and probably frustrated, since the advice wasn't changing anything.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the routine work, and why?
qa.a: Turning each item on the list of ruin into a fixed habit, such as the phone in the other room and past papers every Sunday, made it work, since each risk had a plain answer.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother have felt seeing the list on the wall?
qa.a: Ramesh's mother was probably relieved and a little proud, which is why Ramesh's mother quietly stopped calling for late tea.

The board exams were eight weeks away, and Anjali's younger brother had just started drum classes in the room next to hers. Evenings would be noisy from now on.
She sat on her bed with a notebook and flipped the question around. Not "how do I do well?" but "how would I definitely do badly?"
She wrote fast. Stay up all night before each paper. Sleep five hours. Never touch past papers. Study only on the loud evenings. Keep the phone next to the book.
Her friend Rafiq called. "What are you doing?"
"Making a list of how to fail."
"Very motivating."
"No, listen. Now I just do the opposite." She turned the page. Sleep by eleven. Study the hard subjects in the quiet early mornings. One past paper every Sunday. Phone in the kitchen.
Rafiq was quiet. "Can you send me that list?"

qa.q: Where does Anjali plan to keep her phone?
How did Anjali feel as she turned the page to the opposite list?
qa.a: She felt confident and clear-headed, since knowing exactly what to avoid made the routine easy to write.

qa.q: What else could Anjali add to make the list work, and why?
qa.a: She could add one clear target, like finishing a chapter each week, so the plan works toward something and not only away from mistakes.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Anjali's list?
qa.a: Rafiq first teases that it is not motivating, then sees its value and asks for a copy.

grounding: It shows a student listing what would ruin her exam results, like cramming, no sleep and no past papers, and building a routine to avoid each.

In the Andheri coaching centre's library, Arohi was staring at a blank timetable. Her friend Madhav leaned over. "Still empty?"
"I don't know where to start."
"Then start from the other end. What would guarantee you mess up the boards?"
Arohi thought, then wrote. All-nighters before exams. Skipping breakfast. No practice papers. Starting maths only in February. Studying in bed.
She looked at the list for a minute. "Okay. That's weirdly easy."
Then she wrote the opposite beside each one. Sleep seven hours, no all-nighters. Breakfast before the first session. One past paper every Saturday. Maths from this week. Study at the table only.
She stuck it in her folder. "This I can actually follow."
Madhav grinned. "Now I'm making one."

qa.q: What did Arohi write as the opposite of no practice papers?
How did Arohi feel after listing the ways to mess up?
qa.a: She felt surprised and more confident, calling it weirdly easy and saying she could actually follow the new plan.

qa.q: Which other approach could Arohi add to the inversion list?
qa.a: She could set a small weekly goal, like a mock score to reach, so the plan also moves her toward something.

qa.q: How might Madhav be affected by watching Arohi make the list?
qa.a: Madhav is inspired enough to make his own, seeing how quickly the blank timetable became something useful.

grounding: It shows a student asking what would guarantee failure in exams, listing cramming, skipped sleep and no past papers, and building a routine that avoids each.
